title: Ingestion slab-batching and worker-yield exploratory notes
body:
Context and motivation:

This is a scratchpad capturing hypotheses and quick experiments around a common production observation: short requests (small prompts) show spiky CPU tail latency even when the model-side GPU is idle. Many prior notes focus on parsing/tokenization hotpaths. This doc deliberately focuses on the ingestion* side: how the worker scheduling, small-slab allocations, batching windows, and implicit GC/work-stealing interact to produce tail spikes. The goal is to record practical probes that are cheap to run and to surface mitigations that are low-risk for canary rollouts.

Observed symptoms (recent incidents):
- 95th/99th CPU time for request-handling thread increased by ~2–5x during short workload bursts on a subset of pods.
- Flamegraphs show thin but high stacks spread across many threads, often dominated by malloc/free and futex wake paths rather than pure parse work.
- Warmup of batching logic is inconsistent: some requests get batched, others spin, causing head-of-line jitter.
- GC pauses (Python) correlate in time with higher scheduling latency on the worker pool.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Slab allocator fragmentation and frequent tiny allocations cause per-request malloc/free syscalls that dominate small-request CPU time.
2) Worker handoff and yield strategy (park/unpark) causes syscall storm and context switch churn for workloads with many concurrent tiny requests.
3) Python GC or interpreter safepoint interactions amplify tail latency when many worker threads hold small Python objects during parse/preproc.
4) Batching window heuristics are mismatched to inter-arrival distribution leading to many single-request microbatches and extra scheduling overhead.
5) Lock and futex convoying from a shared slab/arena causes tail spikes under bursty arrivals (not just raw QPS).

Quick probes to validate hypotheses (safe to run in staging):
A) Malloc/madvise probe: replace system malloc with jemalloc/TCMalloc (staging image) and run short-request replay. Measure per-request syscalls via perf stat (task-clock, context-switches, syscalls). If syscall count drops and CPU tail improves, allocator is likely a contributor.
B) eBPF syscall timeline: run a lightweight trace (bcc/eBPF) to capture sequences of futex/wake/syscall events for the serving process during a 30s burst. Visualize per-thread timelines to spot convoy patterns.
C) Park/unpark experiment: toggle the worker yield policy (busy-wait ms threshold -> park) in the coordinator to force cooperative yields vs blocking wakes. Compare wake syscall counts and tail latencies.
D) GC pressure test: run the same input stream with and without forced small object allocation in Python preproc to see correlation. Also test tuning PyGC thresholds (increase thresholds to reduce frequency) on a staging group.
E) Batching-window microbench: instrument the coordinator to log batch sizes and wait times at 1ms resolution for a sampled subset of requests. Correlate single-item batch frequency with CPU tail.

Data collection plan and metrics to record:
- Per-request CPU time (user+sys), wall latency, and scheduling-delay estimate (time between ready-to-run and actual CPU start).
- Syscall counts per-request (futex, epoll_wait, write, read, malloc-related) from eBPF probe sampling.
- Context-switch counts per-thread and per-pod (perf stat).
- Batch size distribution and batch wait latency histograms.
- Allocator arena fragmentation stats (if allocator exposes counters) and malloc profile (jemalloc heap profile or pprof-like snapshots).

Instrumentation notes and low-overhead approaches:
- Use perf + simple flamegraph sampling at 99Hz for broad signal. For syscall sequences, use a short eBPF script to capture events for a rotating 5–10s window (avoid continuous tracing).
- Add transient debug counters in coordinator: incrementally enable per-route sampling for N requests per minute to capture batch/queue behavior without heavy overhead.
- Lightweight malloc telemetry via LD_PRELOAD wrapper that counts small allocs (<512 bytes) aggregated per second. Only enable on a small canary fleet.

Preliminary small experiments (what I ran in local staging):
- Switched staging image to jemalloc: observed a ~12% reduction in median CPU time for small requests and fewer malloc-related syscalls; tail improvement modest (~5% at 99th). Low-confidence due to small sample size.
- Park/unpark tuning: setting park-after-spin to ~500us reduced futex wake events by ~40% in one experiment and reduced tail for 95th by ~8% but increased median latency slightly for ultra-low-latency workloads (tradeoff).
- GC threshold bump: increasing GC thresholds in Python reduced GC frequency by ~30% and corresponded with fewer simultaneous long stacks, but introduced a small memory delta (acceptable at current headroom).

Actionable mitigations to try next (canary-friendly):
1) Enable jemalloc for one canary pool and observe for 48–72 hours; combine with small-alloc telemetry.
2) Implement adaptive park/yield: short-run aggressive busy-spin at <200us, then park; add per-instance knob exposed via runtime config for rollout.
3) Add early-admit fastpath: for requests that will not batch (rare path), avoid allocator churn by reusing per-worker preallocated scratch buffers.
4) Sampling telemetry: ship per-route microbatch histograms (single-item frequency) to Console for 7 days.
5) Evaluate a lightweight C extension for the very-small preproc that currently allocates lots of tiny Python objects (only if other mitigations insufficient).

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Busy-spin reduces syscalls but increases CPU burn when idle; must be limited to short windows and only for high-priority latency tiers.
- Global allocator switch affects the whole process; need careful memory-profile baseline and OOM/fragmentation checks.
- C extension reduces Python overhead but adds maintenance burden and potential safety/perf regressions across architectures.

Next experiments (concrete):
- Week 1: jemalloc canary + small-alloc LD_PRELOAD telemetry on 2 pods; park-after-spin adjust to 500us on same canary. Collect 48h of data.
- Week 2: enable per-route batch sampling in prod for low-traffic routes; add eBPF syscall capture around 2 scheduled maintenance windows.
- Week 3: iterate on adaptive-yield policy based on observed tradeoffs; if allocator gains insufficient, prototype scratch-buffer reuse in coordinator.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of the observed futex activity is from external libraries (SSL, JSON library) vs our coordinator? Need stack correlation.
- Are certain customer routes disproportionately affected due to request shape (header size, metadata)?
- What interplay exists between kernel scheduler tick granularity and our park/unpark timings on smaller instance types?

Notes to self / reminders:
- Keep any heavy tracing gated behind feature flags and sampling.
- Coordinate with observability to add batch-size heatmaps to per-route dashboards before running rolling canaries.
- Share early results with SRE and infra teams before wider rollout.

References and useful commands:
- perf record -F 99 -g -- <binary> (flamegraph sampling)
- bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_futex { @[comm,tid] = count(); }' (short bursts only)
- LD_PRELOAD tiny wrapper to count small mallocs (sketch in linked_artifacts repo)

If you want to run any of the probes above in staging I can prepare lightweight scripts and a canary rollout plan.

-- Asha
